name: MonarchKbd
title: Kbd
wrapsNative: Text on a filled RoundedRectangle; GCKeyboard (GameController) to know whether a hardware keyboard is attached
summary: A keyboard key or shortcut drawn as a key cap, such as ⌘K. By default it is drawn only while a hardware keyboard is attached.
whenToUse: Beside a command that has a keyboard shortcut, as a hint for people who use a hardware keyboard, and in a list of shortcuts (with isAlwaysVisible).
whenNotToUse: Do not use it to define a shortcut; that is keyboardShortcut(_:modifiers:) on the control, which also lists the shortcut in the system's shortcut overlay on iPad. Not for code; use MonarchInlineCodeStyle.
api: init(_ keys: String, labels: MonarchKbdLabels = MonarchKbdLabels(), isAlwaysVisible: Bool = false)

struct MonarchKbdLabels { init(command: String? = nil, shift: String? = nil, option: String? = nil, control: String? = nil, return: String? = nil, escape: String? = nil, delete: String? = nil, tab: String? = nil, space: String? = nil, capsLock: String? = nil, upArrow: String? = nil, downArrow: String? = nil, leftArrow: String? = nil, rightArrow: String? = nil) }

options.name: keys
options.description: The key or shortcut as it is shown, such as "⌘K", "Esc" or "⇧⌘P".

options.name: labels
options.description: Replacements for the names VoiceOver reads for the key glyphs ⌘ ⇧ ⌥ ⌃ ↩ ⎋ ⌫ ⇥ ␣ ⇪ ↑ ↓ ← →.

options.name: isAlwaysVisible
options.description: Draw the cap without a hardware keyboard too.

states.name: no keyboard
states.description: Nothing is drawn and the view takes no room, unless isAlwaysVisible is true. The cap appears and disappears as a keyboard is attached and detached.

appearance: Muted text in the code role on the subtle background colour, with a border in the default border colour that is two points thick at the bottom, in a 4-point rounded rectangle. The roles are the same in light, dark and both high-contrast themes.
platformNotes: The web Kbd is always visible, because a browser cannot tell whether a keyboard is present; on iOS the hint is hidden on a device without one. The web text is 11 pixels; iOS uses the code role (14 points before Dynamic Type) because smaller text is not legible on a phone. The spoken key names are an iOS addition: a browser leaves the glyphs to the screen reader. Android has the same component.
accessibility: The cap is one accessibility element whose label names the keys: "⇧⌘P" is read as "Shift Command P".
Characters that are not key glyphs are read as written, so "Esc" and "Ctrl+K" are unchanged.
The text scales with Dynamic Type and the smallest size of the cap scales with it.
The cap is not interactive and has no traits.
The key is shown by a border and a shape, not by colour alone.
edgeCases: Whether a keyboard is attached comes from GCKeyboard.coalesced and its connect and disconnect notifications. On the macOS host and in the simulator with "Connect Hardware Keyboard" a keyboard is reported.
A HStack with spacing still adds its spacing beside a hidden cap, because the view stays in the layout to watch for a keyboard.
Long text wraps inside the cap and is centred.
An empty string draws an empty cap of the smallest size.
